items.abstract: <jats:p>The proliferation of desktop digital manufacturing equipment and the advancement of AIdriven autonomous decision-making have created technological conditions for extending manufacturing activities from centralized factories to household units. However, existing research predominantly focuses on tool accessibility and innovation motivation, implicitly assuming that users possess specialized skills, and thus fails to address how ordinary individuals can accomplish product fabrication without professional expertise. To fill this gap, this paper proposes the "Home Making" (HM) paradigm, which centers on an AI Agent substituting for human decision-making in manufacturing to achieve a continuous decrement in human intervention throughout the manufacturing process-thereby distinguishing itself from the toolaccessibility-centric analytical approach of prior studies. The research constructs a four-stage evolutionary model and a seven-link framework, and defines the "Delegation Threshold" (DT) as a quantifiable grading criterion for paradigm maturity; it further designs and implements a cloud-edge-terminal three-tier network architecture, establishes a cross-platform communication mechanism based on FastDDS and WSS protocols, and builds a prototype system infrastructure. Verification results demonstrate stable communication links, with both autonomous email notification and basic Web console functionalities passing usability tests. The theoretical contribution of this paper lies in shifting the research perspective from "humans operating tools" to "humans delegating to the system," providing an extensible conceptual framework and a technical reference architecture. Its practical significance resides in lowering the skill barriers for individuals to accomplish product fabrication, thereby laying a foundation for the extension of manufacturing capabilities to distributed household units.</jats:p>
title: The Home Making Paradigm: A Conceptual Framework with Prototype Validation

items.abstract: <jats:p><p>Traditional FICO-based mortgage underwriting systematically excludes recently arrived immigrants who lack domestic credit history, even when their income, educational credentials, and housing payment behaviour indicate strong creditworthiness. This study applies a Random Forest machine learning framework to develop and validate the Human Capital Wealth Capacity Index (HC-WCI), an AI-augmented alternative qualification tool built on three publicly observable variables: educational attainment, years of U.S. residency, and a geospatially normalised Rent Performance Ratio. Using American Community Survey (ACS) microdata covering 166 million weighted person-observations across ten immigrant national-origin groups, a four-model machine learning comparison shows that human capital variables explain 14.0% of cohort-level mortgage rate variation, compared with 5.6% for income alone. Two supplementary datasets are used to validate the framework's central claims. American Housing Survey (AHS) 2023 data confirm that renters in the highest Rent Performance Ratio quartile face a late payment rate of 4.65%, compared with 8.64% in the lowest quartile (χ²=59.73, p&lt;0.001). Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) data from 2016 to 2022 show that credit exclusion rates fall monotonically from 29.6% among households with some high school education to 8.5% among college graduates. Together, the findings provide an empirical foundation for incorporating machine learning-derived human capital signals into U.S. mortgage underwriting and offer a practical AI-assisted pre-screening tool for identifying credit-invisible immigrant households that current models systematically misclassify.</p></jats:p>
title: A Machine Learning Framework for Human Capital-Based Mortgage Qualification: Evidence from U.S. Immigrant Borrower Cohorts

items.abstract: Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) systems combine safety-relevant telemetry, wireless communication, distributed identity, collaborative learning, and long-lived cryptographic trust, creating security dependencies that are difficult to evaluate when each mechanism is studied in isolation. This paper presents OmniGuard V2X, a six-layer research prototype that integrates post-quantum key establishment and signatures, privacy commitments, decentralized identity, a permissioned tamper-evident ledger, federated-learning experimentation, anomaly hooks, and authenticated runtime services in a unified C++/Go/Python stack. The contribution is an assumption-aware validation model rather than a new cryptographic primitive. The supported native path uses real ML-KEM-512 and ML-DSA-44 operations, while classical Pedersen and Schnorr-style assumptions are explicitly excluded from end-to-end post-quantum claims. The prototype further implements encrypted persistent PQC identity material, stable key identifiers, guarded rotation, signed key-transition evidence, bounded historical signature verification, fail-closed provider selection, replay-aware local control, and authenticated rollback-state checks. A retained warm-start pipeline measurement is 5.34 ms in one prototype environment and is reported only as a descriptive local result. Existing anomaly and federated-learning experiments are classified as sanity checks because they do not yet support statistically defensible robustness metrics. The study shows how machine-readable security boundaries and evidence-aware claim control can improve the reproducibility and interpretability of multi-mechanism V2X security prototypes.
title: OmniGuard V2X: A Hybrid-Security Prototype Framework with Assumption-Aware Validation for Smart Vehicle Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Central bank digital currency (CBDC) has increasingly received attention among policymakers and academics. From a theoretical perspective, the introduction of a CBDC arouses long-standing questions, foreseeing the possibility for the private (non-financial) sector to access the central bank’s reserves. The aim of this paper is to strengthen the understanding of the CBDC through the Endogenous Money Theory (EMT). The paper examines the balance sheets of the central bank, commercial banks, and non-financial private system, tracking all the assets and liabilities of the macro-agents involved in the introduction of a central bank digital currency. It explains the logical chain of relationships starting with the creation of bank loans from commercial banks, transformed into deposits and ultimately converted into central bank digital currency. Such a chain of relationships is studied and explained also by adapting the four quadrants model proposed by many post-Keynesian scholars.</jats:p>
title: The Interpretation of CBDC within an Endogenous Money Framework

items.abstract: <jats:p>We present the first empirical evidence on how a live retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) affects bank funding, lending, and payments, using the rollout of India’s digital rupee. Exploiting quasi-experimental variation from the Reserve Bank of India’s staggered authorization of lead banks and centrally coordinated CBDC marketing campaigns at a large public-sector bank, we show that CBDC eligibility reduces retail deposits by 2.7%, concentrated in liquid savings accounts, while illiquid term deposits remain unchanged. Credit falls initially but quickly recovers, consistent with banks adjusting their funding mix. On the payments side, CBDC crowds out deposit-backed digital rails rather than cash usage. Early adoption is skewed toward wealthier, uninsured, and more educated depositors. A simple sufficient-statistics framework implies that the net welfare effect is positive, with household convenience and safety gains outweighing the costs of lost deposit franchise value, temporary credit contraction, and more expensive wholesale funding.</jats:p>
title: Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC), Bank Deposits, and Digital Payments: First Evidence from a Live Retail CBDC

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The Electric sail concept is based on a distributed tether satellite system with tether lengths on the order of thousands-of meters. The system must deploy from stowed arrangement into a selected flight configuration in which thrust forces are transmitted through the tether to the satellite body. The system must be stable through deployment procedure and maintain stable, desired configuration during flight operations. Understanding the dynamic behavior of the satellite bodies and distributed, conductive tether are critical to long-range design and development of the Electric Sail concept. This paper’s contribution is the presentation, development and validation of a mathematical model for simulating E-Sail deployment of a prototype system for testing on the MSFC Robotic Flat Floor Facility. A massed tether model is developed using the bead and string concept with equations of motion derived from Lagrange’s Method. The model is validated using infrared motion capture data produced by controlled experiments of a representative tether portion outfitted with IR targets. Further, a prototype is presented which will be used to investigate an E-Sail deployment approach and associated control. The design of this system will allow for deployment on specially designed flat floor facilities at MSFC. The prototype will be used to: 1) gather data for validation of system dynamic model, 2) evaluate alternative deployment strategies, 3) evaluate tether reel-out and damping control strategies.</jats:p>
title: Modeling, Validation and Prototype Development of Electric Sail Tether Deployment Systems for CubeSats

items.abstract: <jats:p>We analyse the impact of introducing a central bank-issued digital currency (CBDC) on the operational framework of monetary policy and the macroeconomy as a whole. To this end, we develop a New Keynesian model with heterogeneous banks, a frictional interbank market, a central bank with deposit and lending facilities, and household preferences for different liquid assets. The model is calibrated to replicate the main monetary and financial aggregates in the euro area. Our analysis predicts that CBDC adoption implies a roughly equivalent reduction in banks’ deposit funding. However, this ‘deposit crunch’ has a rather small effect on bank lending to the real economy, and hence on aggregate investment and GDP. This result reflects the parallel impact of a CBDC on a central bank’s operational framework. For relatively moderate CBDC adoption levels, the reduction in deposits is absorbed by an almost one-to-one fall in reserves at the central bank, implying a transition from a ‘floor’ system – with ample reserves – to a ‘corridor’ system. For larger CBDC adoption, the loss of bank deposits is compensated by increased recourse to central bank credit, as the corridor system gives way to a ‘ceiling’ system with scarce reserves.</jats:p>
title: CBDC and the Operational Framework of Monetary Policy

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates the impact of China's e-CNY pilot on the nonperforming loans (NPLs) of Chinese banks. The findings show that the e-CNY pilot is associated with a significant reduction in NPLs. The effect is observed across banks of all sizes, with larger banks experiencing the strongest improvement in asset quality. When analyzed by bank type, the e-CNY pilot significantly lowers NPLs for joint-stock commercial banks, urban commercial banks, rural commercial banks, foreign-funded banks, and rural credit cooperatives, with the greatest impact seen among rural commercial banks. Conversely, NPLs of policy banks, large state-owned banks, and new rural financial institutions show no significant change. These findings suggest that the introduction of a central bank digital currency can enhance banks' credit quality while posing no adverse effects on loan performance, providing valuable guidance for policymakers considering CBDC implementation.</jats:p>
title: CBDC Pilot and Banks' Non-Performing Loans: Evidence from China

items.abstract: <jats:p>We characterize the conditions under which asymmetries in interbank markets collapse, and show that this occurs only when both matching frictions and corridor-based policy wedges are absent. Across three distinct modeling environments-efficient matching, a zero standing-facility corridor, and reduced two-type banking structures-the steady state converges to the same set of interest-rate equalities linking interbank, lending, and deposit rates to the return on reserves. This convergence arises despite substantial differences in the underlying frictions. The analysis clarifies when three-type bank heterogeneity can emerge and shows that non-participation requires either matching inefficiency or a positive policy corridor. These findings refine the theoretical foundations of interbank market modeling in CBDC frameworks and help explain why seemingly different models often deliver identical steady-state outcomes.</jats:p>
title: When Do Interbank Market Asymmetries Disappear? Evidence from CBDC Models
